title: Around a Freshwater Pond
description: Explore the shallow edge of a freshwater pond, where plants, insects, and amphibians share a small habitat.
cardDescription: Explore the shallow edge of a freshwater pond, where plants, insects, and amphibians share a small habitat.
focus: The scene distinguishes an animal from its young and a waterside plant from its growing place. Some pond creatures change shape as they develop.
solvingTip: Use the habitat and body description together. A life-stage clue calls for a stage name rather than the adult animal.
words: Leaping amphibian often heard calling beside a pond
Aquatic young frog before its adult legs fully develop
Long-bodied flying insect often hovering over pond water
Wetland plant with a dense brown cylindrical flower head
Small amphibian with a tail retained as an adult
Tall grasslike waterside plant with a hollow or jointed stem
Slow-moving pond animal with a coiled shell
Small body of still fresh water in this scene
Sloping land at the edge of the water
Wet soft earth beneath a pond visitor's boots
Early life stage laid in water by many frogs
One of the paired flight surfaces on an adult pond insect
Flat green plant part floating at the water's surface

answerNotes.FROG: A frog is an amphibian. Its young commonly begin life as aquatic tadpoles, though frog life cycles vary.
answerNotes.TADPOLE: A tadpole is a life stage, not a separate species. In a typical frog life cycle, its body changes as it develops.
answerNotes.DRAGONFLY: A dragonfly has aquatic young and a flying adult stage. It is an insect, unlike a frog or snail.
answerNotes.CATTAIL: Cattails grow in wetlands and have long narrow leaves. The distinctive brown head helps identify the plant in this clue.
answerNotes.NEWT: A newt is a kind of salamander. An adult frog usually lacks the long tail that a newt keeps.

title: A Honeybee Colony
description: Look inside the vocabulary of a honeybee colony, from its wax chambers to the different bees that live together.
cardDescription: Look inside the vocabulary of a honeybee colony, from its wax chambers to the different bees that live together.
focus: These clues concern honeybees rather than every bee species. The names for colony members describe different biological roles, and food words distinguish floral ingredients from stored products.
solvingTip: Separate the insect’s role from the material or structure. Use the short hive words to cross longer flower-related answers.
words: Principal egg-laying female in a honeybee colony
Female honeybee that gathers food and maintains the colony
Structure of adjoining wax chambers built by honeybees
Sweet floral liquid collected by honeybees
Home or enclosure occupied by a honeybee colony
Sweet food made and stored by honeybees
Material honeybees use to construct their hexagonal chambers
Collective term for a colony's developing young
Flower powder collected as a protein source by honeybees
One hexagonal chamber in a honeybee's wax structure
Group of bees leaving together to establish a new colony
Defensive piercing structure on a female honeybee
Thin flight surface on the side of a honeybee's body

answerNotes.QUEEN: A queen's central role is reproduction. The name does not mean she directs colony activity like a human ruler.
answerNotes.DRONE: Drone identifies the male. Worker honeybees are female and perform many of the colony's everyday tasks.
answerNotes.WORKER: Worker honeybees carry out different jobs as they mature. They are distinct from the colony's principal egg-laying queen.
answerNotes.COMB: Comb contains cells used for food storage and developing young. The structure is different from the hive enclosing the colony.
answerNotes.NECTAR: Nectar supplies sugars. Pollen is the powdery material associated with a flower's male reproductive structures.

title: Caterpillars and Cocoons
description: Follow the names used for the stages of butterflies and moths, including the difference between a pupa and its covering.
cardDescription: Follow the names used for the stages of butterflies and moths, including the difference between a pupa and its covering.
focus: A life stage and an enclosing structure are different things. The clues make that distinction explicit while connecting familiar flying insects with their younger forms.
solvingTip: Read whether a definition asks for a stage, a covering, or a body part. Those categories help separate similar insect words.
words: Immature feeding stage represented by a caterpillar
Insect life stage between larva and adult in complete metamorphosis
Name commonly given to a butterfly's pupa
Protective silk covering spun by many moth caterpillars
Fine fiber a caterpillar may spin into a protective case
Life stage from which a caterpillar hatches
One of an adult moth's paired head feelers
Six-legged animal group containing moths and butterflies
Adult butterfly body part bearing tiny colored scales
Flying insect whose caterpillar may spin a silk case
To eat leaves, as a growing caterpillar does
To increase in size during a caterpillar's feeding stage
One distinct period in an insect's life cycle
Adult insect whose pupa is commonly called a chrysalis

answerNotes.LARVA: Larva is the stage name. Caterpillar is the familiar term for the larva of a butterfly or moth.
answerNotes.PUPA: A pupa is the developing insect, not a silk case around it. Changes to the adult form occur during this stage.
answerNotes.CHRYSALIS: A chrysalis is a butterfly pupa. It should not be confused with a cocoon, which is an outer silk covering.
answerNotes.COCOON: A cocoon encloses a pupa. Many moths make one, but a cocoon is not part of every moth's life cycle.
answerNotes.SILK: Silk is the fiber used for a cocoon. The insect inside is called a pupa.

title: Rings on a Tree Stump
description: Look at a cut tree stump through its rings, bark, shape, and familiar wood words.
cardDescription: Look at a cut tree stump through its rings, bark, shape, and familiar wood words.
focus: A cut tree can show growth rings. Their number can help estimate age, while the bark covers the outside.
solvingTip: Begin with a visible shape or tree part.
words: Part of a tree trunk left after the upper tree is cut
One growth band visible at the cut end of a tree
How old the tree was when it was cut
Rough outer covering around the stump
Main woody part rising above the tree's roots
Hard material exposed at the stump's top
Tree part extending into the ground
Toothed tool used to cut a tree branch or trunk
Separate wood with a sharp tool
Add up the visible growth bands one by one
Shaped like a circle, as many cut stumps appear
Twelve-month period used to describe a tree's age
Length of tree trunk cut for use as wood
Central part of the cut tree section

answerNotes.STUMP: A stump is the remaining lower trunk, rather than a whole standing tree.
answerNotes.RING: Growth rings can help estimate a tree's age; their appearance varies with conditions.
answerNotes.AGE: Ring counts can help estimate age, rather than give a tree's name.
answerNotes.BARK: Bark is on the outside, while growth rings are seen in the cut wood.
answerNotes.TRUNK: A stump is the lower portion left from this main stem.

title: Animal Tracks in Mud
description: Examine the vocabulary of footprints and trails left by familiar animals near a muddy path.
cardDescription: Examine the vocabulary of footprints and trails left by familiar animals near a muddy path.
focus: A mark can suggest the kind of foot that made it. These clues describe vocabulary and recognizable features; an actual identification can also depend on size, movement, and surrounding signs.
solvingTip: Check whether the clue names an animal, a foot part, a single mark, or a sequence of marks. The category narrows the possibilities.
words: Mark left on the ground by an animal's foot
Hard foot covering that can leave a deer's split impression
Curved pointed nail that may show ahead of a toe print
Masked mammal whose forefeet can leave handlike impressions
Pattern of movement revealed by a sequence of footprints
Impression pressed into soft ground by a foot
Soft-footed animal's foot, as on a fox
One digit that may leave a small impression
Sequence of marks showing an animal's route
Soft wet ground that can hold clear footprints
Loose grains that may preserve a passing animal's marks
Bushy-tailed wild canine that leaves paw marks
Hoofed woodland mammal often seen near a meadow
Long-eared animal that commonly moves by hopping
Joined by skin between the toes, as many swimming birds' feet are

answerNotes.TRACK: A track is one sign of an animal's passage. A trail can include a succession of such marks.
answerNotes.HOOF: Deer have cloven hooves. A hoof impression differs from the paw print of a fox or raccoon.
answerNotes.CLAW: Claw marks can help describe a print, but their presence alone does not identify every animal reliably.
answerNotes.RACCOON: A raccoon's front tracks often suggest small hands. Several features together are more useful than one isolated resemblance.
answerNotes.GAIT: Gait concerns how an animal moves, such as walking or bounding. It is different from the shape of one print.
